subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Eduqas spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Eduqas Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Diffusion is best described as the net movement of particles:
options: From a high to a low concentration, down a concentration gradient
From a low to a high concentration, using energy
Only across a partially permeable membrane
questions.explain: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration (down the gradient). It is passive and needs no energy from respiration.

questions.q: Which change would INCREASE the rate of diffusion across a surface?
questions.explain: Rate of diffusion increases with a larger surface area, a greater concentration difference, a shorter diffusion distance and a higher temperature.

questions.q: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules:
options: From a concentrated to a dilute solution using energy
From a dilute to a concentrated solution across a partially permeable membrane
questions.explain: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (high water concentration) to a concentrated solution (low water concentration) across a partially permeable membrane.

questions.q: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens?
options: It loses water and becomes flaccid
It gains water by osmosis and becomes turgid
questions.explain: In pure water, water enters the plant cell by osmosis. The cell becomes turgid; the cell wall prevents it bursting. In animal cells (no wall) this can cause lysis.

questions.q: How does active transport differ from diffusion?
options: It moves particles down the gradient
It moves particles against the concentration gradient and uses energy from respiration
questions.explain: Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient (low to high) and requires energy released by respiration - unlike passive diffusion or osmosis.

questions.q: Root hair cells absorb mineral ions from soil where ion concentration is LOWER than inside the cell. This requires:
questions.explain: Because ions move from low (soil) to high (cell) concentration, against the gradient, root hair cells use active transport, which needs energy from respiration.

questions.q: As an organism gets larger, its surface area to volume ratio:
questions.explain: As size increases, volume grows faster than surface area, so the SA:V ratio decreases. Large organisms therefore need specialised exchange and transport systems.

questions.q: Why do large, multicellular organisms need transport systems rather than relying on diffusion alone?
options: Their small SA:V ratio and large size make diffusion too slow to supply all cells
questions.explain: Large organisms have a small SA:V ratio and long diffusion distances, so simple diffusion is too slow to meet demand. Transport systems move substances quickly to and from all cells.

questions.q: Which feature makes an exchange surface such as an alveolus efficient?
options: A large surface area and a thin, moist membrane
questions.explain: Efficient exchange surfaces have a large surface area, a thin membrane (short diffusion path), a good blood supply and are moist - maximising the rate of diffusion.

questions.q: What is the main function of red blood cells?
questions.explain: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin, transporting oxygen around the body. They have no nucleus and a biconcave shape for maximum surface area.

questions.q: Which blood component is mainly responsible for clotting at a wound?
questions.explain: Platelets are cell fragments that trigger blood clotting, forming a plug and network that seals wounds and prevents pathogen entry and blood loss.

questions.q: Which blood vessel carries blood AWAY from the heart at high pressure?
questions.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick, muscular, elastic walls. Veins return blood at low pressure and have valves; capillaries allow exchange.

questions.q: Which feature helps veins return blood to the heart against gravity?
questions.explain: Veins contain valves that prevent backflow, helping blood return to the heart at low pressure. They have relatively thin walls and a wide lumen.

questions.q: Humans have a double circulatory system. What does this mean?
options: Blood passes through the heart once per full circuit
Blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit of the body
questions.explain: In a double circulatory system, blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: once to the lungs (pulmonary) and once to the body (systemic), maintaining high pressure.

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood out to the body via the aorta?
questions.explain: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood at high pressure through the aorta to the body. It has the thickest muscular wall. The right ventricle pumps to the lungs.

questions.q: Which tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves?
questions.explain: Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral ions upwards from roots to leaves in the transpiration stream. It is made of dead, hollow cells strengthened with lignin.

questions.q: What does the phloem transport?
options: Dissolved sugars (e.g. sucrose) made in photosynthesis, in translocation
questions.explain: Phloem transports dissolved sugars (such as sucrose) from the leaves to other parts of the plant for use or storage - a process called translocation. It uses living cells.

questions.q: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant mainly through the:
questions.explain: Transpiration is the evaporation and diffusion of water vapour from the leaves, mostly through the stomata (usually on the lower surface), driving the transpiration stream.

questions.q: Which condition would INCREASE the rate of transpiration?
questions.explain: Transpiration increases with higher temperature, lower humidity, increased air movement (wind) and higher light intensity (stomata open). Wind removes water vapour, steepening the gradient.

questions.q: (Higher tier) A potometer measures water uptake by a shoot. It is often used as an estimate of transpiration rate because:
options: Most water taken up is lost by transpiration
All water taken up is stored in the roots
Water uptake and transpiration are unrelated
questions.explain: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake, which closely approximates transpiration because most of the water absorbed is lost as vapour through the leaves.
